case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Maryland appellate court unreasonably applied clearly established Supreme Court Brady materiality precedent (as constrained by AEDPA) by effectively treating materiality as a sufficiency-of-the-evidence inquiry rather than assessing the suppressed impeachment/exculpatory evidence cumulatively and in context of the whole case.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1) (AEDPA—“contrary to” or “unreasonable application” of clearly established federal law) as applied to the Due Process Brady obligation (U.S. Const. amend. XIV) requiring disclosure of material exculpatory/impeachment evidence.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The State (Klein, Superintendent, et al.) argues that the suppressed evidence was not “material” under Brady because, even accounting for it, the remaining trial evidence was sufficient to sustain the verdict; it relies in part on Strickler to contend that impeachment of a key witness would not have changed the outcome and that the state court’s no-materiality determination was at least reasonable under AEDPA’s deferential standard.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Martin argues that clearly established Supreme Court law—especially Kyles—requires a holistic, cumulative materiality analysis that (1) adds the suppressed evidence to the defense case and (2) subtracts the force of the prosecution case by accounting for how impeachment would weaken key testimony; he contends the Maryland appellate court unreasonably applied that rule by listing evidence supporting guilt (a sufficiency-style analysis) rather than evaluating how suppressed impeachment of Carter would have undermined the prosecution’s theory, other evidence, and the overall trial narrative, making Strickler factually distinguishable.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito rightly stress Richter’s “fairminded disagreement” bar and that Kyles permits considering the remaining strength of the State’s case as part of the overall inquiry. But Kyles clearly establishes a methodological constraint: materiality is a cumulative, whole-case “reasonable probability” assessment and is “not a sufficiency of evidence test,” and a state court unreasonably applies Brady when it effectively treats “substantial evidence of guilt” as dispositive rather than grappling with how the suppressed impeachment would alter the narrative presented to the jury. Strickler does not dilute Kyles; it applies the same standard on different facts and therefore cannot justify collapsing materiality into a sufficiency-style tally. I would therefore adhere to a narrow AEDPA holding—limited to cases where the state court’s reasoning, despite reciting Brady’s words, functionally substitutes sufficiency review for Kyles’s required cumulative analysis—so we respect deference while enforcing our clearly established rule.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: I take seriously Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s point that Kyles clearly rejects a sufficiency-of-the-evidence substitution for Brady materiality and that methodology can matter even when the right standard is recited. But under AEDPA as construed in Harrington v. Richter, our task is not to police analytic style; it is to ask whether the state court’s no-materiality judgment—having stated the correct “reasonable probability” rule—was objectively unreasonable beyond fairminded disagreement, and consideration of the remaining evidence is not per se forbidden by Kyles when done as part of the whole-case inquiry. Strickler reinforces that impeachment evidence often will not undermine confidence where other proof substantially corroborates guilt, and nothing in Kyles clearly establishes that a state court’s emphasis on corroborating proof, without more, necessarily crosses § 2254(d)(1)’s high bar. Unless the record shows the state court treated “substantial evidence remains” as dispositive (not merely relevant), I cannot say its application was an extreme malfunction warranting habeas relief.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that Kyles clearly forbids collapsing Brady materiality into a sufficiency-of-the-evidence test, and that a state court can unreasonably apply clearly established law even while reciting the right words. But under Richter and Williams, § 2254(d)(1) does not authorize us to police the elegance of a state court’s methodology so long as the court identified the governing “reasonable probability” rule and reached a bottom-line no-materiality determination that remains within fairminded disagreement on this record. Kyles permits considering the strength of the remaining case as part of the holistic inquiry, and Strickler confirms that withheld impeachment often will not undermine confidence where other evidence substantially corroborates guilt—so the “substantial evidence” discussion does not necessarily show a forbidden sufficiency substitution. Justice Sotomayor’s narrative-reframing critique depends on reading the Maryland decision as making remaining evidence dispositive; given AEDPA’s high bar and the practical finality concerns in habeas, I cannot say the state court’s application was objectively unreasonable rather than, at most, debatable error.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito’s best point is Richter/Williams: AEDPA does not permit relief for mere error, and a state court may consider the strength of the remaining evidence. But Chief Justice Roberts persuasively frames Kyles as clearly establishing not just the words but the method—materiality is “not a sufficiency of evidence test,” and an analysis that effectively treats “substantial evidence remains” as dispositive is an unreasonable application even if it recites “reasonable probability.” Strickler does not dilute Kyles into a sufficiency-like tally; it applies the same confidence-undermining inquiry and still requires assessing how suppressed impeachment would reconfigure the jury’s evaluation of the State’s case. Given the alleged centrality of the suppressed report to impeaching a key link in the State’s narrative, insulating a sufficiency-substitute approach would both misapply Kyles and disproportionately risk wrongful convictions where credibility is decisive.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito are right to foreground Richter’s “fairminded disagreement” bar and the need to tolerate imperfect state-court reasoning, and Strickler confirms that some impeachment nondisclosure is not material where the overall evidentiary picture is largely unchanged. But Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh identify the key limiting principle from Kyles: materiality is a cumulative, whole-case reasonable-probability inquiry and “is not a sufficiency of evidence test,” so a state court can unreasonably apply clearly established law when it recites the right words yet functionally treats “substantial evidence remains” as dispositive. Under my pragmatic textualism, § 2254(d)(1) deference does not extend to a method Kyles expressly rejects; requiring the state court to stay in Kyles’s analytical lane is a workable, narrow rule that preserves AEDPA while enforcing coherence in our Brady jurisprudence. On this framing, the opposing side’s deference argument fails because it would insulate an approach that collapses the required inquiry into a verdict-supporting tally rather than asking how the suppressed impeachment reshapes the case.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito correctly press Richter’s “fairminded disagreement” constraint, and I agree AEDPA does not permit relief for imperfectly written state-court opinions. But Chief Justice Roberts’s point is the decisive one for me: Kyles clearly establishes a methodological rule that Brady materiality is a cumulative “reasonable probability” inquiry and “not a sufficiency of the evidence test,” and a state court unreasonably applies that rule if it functionally treats the existence of “substantial” remaining inculpatory evidence as dispositive rather than asking whether the suppressed evidence, considered with the rest, undermines confidence in the verdict. Strickler does not weaken Kyles; it applies the same standard and thus cannot justify substituting a sufficiency-style tally for the required holistic analysis. Given the claim that the suppressed report undercuts a unique link in the State’s narrative, I cannot say the state court stayed within Kyles’s analytical lane in a way Richter insulates.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito’s strongest point is Richter: AEDPA does not allow relief for mere analytical imperfection, and a state court may consider the strength of the remaining evidence. But Chief Justice Roberts persuasively grounds the limit in clearly established law—Kyles makes materiality a cumulative, whole-case reasonable-probability inquiry and explicitly rejects a sufficiency-of-the-evidence substitute—so a state court that functionally treats “substantial evidence of guilt remains” as dispositive unreasonably applies Brady even if it recites the right words. Strickler, as Roberts and Kagan note, does not relax Kyles; it applies the same framework on facts where the withheld impeachment did not reconfigure the narrative, and thus cannot justify a methodology that sidesteps the holistic cumulative assessment. Given that framing, I do not think Thomas’s deference argument defeats relief when the state court’s mode of analysis crosses Kyles’s clearly established methodological boundary.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito’s strongest point is AEDPA’s Richter/Williams deference: even a thin or imperfect explanation is tolerable if the state court’s bottom-line no-materiality conclusion is within fairminded disagreement. But Chief Justice Roberts is right that Kyles clearly establishes a methodological constraint—materiality is a cumulative “reasonable probability” inquiry and “not a sufficiency of the evidence test”—and a court unreasonably applies Brady when it functionally treats the existence of “substantial evidence” as dispositive without grappling with how the suppressed evidence would have altered the jury’s understanding of the State’s narrative. Strickler, as Justice Kagan notes, does not dilute Kyles into a sufficiency review; it applies the same standard to a record where the withheld impeachment did not meaningfully reframe the case, so it cannot justify a methodology Kyles forbids. Richter’s deference does not extend to insulating a state court’s use of the wrong test in substance, and on this record the alleged sufficiency-like analysis places the decision outside Kyles’s required analytical lane.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito’s Richter point is the hardest: AEDPA bars relief for mere analytical slippage if the bottom-line no-materiality determination remains within fairminded disagreement. But as Chief Justice Roberts explains, Kyles clearly establishes not just the verbal standard (“reasonable probability”) but a prohibition on substituting a sufficiency-style “substantial evidence remains” rationale for the cumulative, narrative-altering materiality inquiry; that kind of methodological swap can itself be an unreasonable application under § 2254(d)(1) even if the court recites the right words. Strickler, which Thomas invokes, reinforces that impeachment is not automatically material, but it does not authorize a state court to avoid assessing how credibility impeachment of a key witness could reconfigure the jury’s evaluation of the whole case. Given the procedural-fairness stakes in Brady and the practical consequence of insulating a forbidden mode of analysis, I remain with Respondent.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under AEDPA, a state court decision is reversible only if it is “contrary to” or an “unreasonable application” of clearly established Supreme Court law. 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1); Williams v. Taylor. Kyles makes clear that Brady materiality requires a cumulative, whole-case inquiry into whether there is a “reasonable probability” of a different result and “is not a sufficiency of evidence test,” 514 U.S. at 434; a state court that effectively reverts to a sufficiency-style accounting unreasonably applies that governing rule even if it recites the correct standard. Given that the suppressed evidence here is asserted to impeach a central prosecution witness and reshape the overall trial narrative, Kyles (and not Strickler’s more fact-bound assessment) supplies the clearly established framework the Maryland appellate court was required to apply.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Under 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1), a federal court may grant relief only if the state court’s decision was not merely wrong, but an objectively “unreasonable application” of clearly established Supreme Court law. Although Kyles v. Whitley instructs that Brady materiality “is not a sufficiency of evidence test” and requires considering suppressed evidence cumulatively and in the context of the whole case, AEDPA permits state courts latitude so long as they apply the correct governing rule in substance. On this record, the Maryland appellate court articulated the Brady materiality standard and concluded the suppressed impeachment/exculpatory evidence did not create a “reasonable probability” of a different result; even if its reasoning emphasized remaining inculpatory proof, that is at most error, not the kind of extreme malfunction Harrington v. Richter describes as required to overcome AEDPA deference. Given that Strickler v. Greene confirms that impeachment evidence is not material where the verdict remains reliably supported, the state court’s no-materiality determination was not beyond the bounds of fairminded disagreement.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Under AEDPA, a federal court may grant relief only if the state court’s decision was not merely incorrect but an “unreasonable application” of clearly established law. 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1); Harrington v. Richter. Although Kyles states that Brady materiality is “not a sufficiency of evidence test,” a state court does not act unreasonably simply by emphasizing the strength of the remaining evidence so long as it ultimately asks whether there is a reasonable probability of a different result, and Strickler illustrates that impeachment evidence often will not meet that standard where the record contains substantial corroboration. Given the deferential Richter/Williams framework and the practical consequences for finality and law enforcement, fairminded jurists could agree with Maryland’s no-materiality determination, so federal habeas relief is unwarranted.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Under Brady and Kyles, suppressed impeachment/exculpatory evidence is “material” when there is a reasonable probability of a different result, assessed cumulatively and in the context of the whole case—not by asking whether the remaining evidence is still sufficient to convict. By effectively tallying “substantial evidence” of guilt and treating materiality as a sufficiency-of-the-evidence inquiry, the Maryland appellate court unreasonably applied clearly established law within the meaning of 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1), especially where the suppressed report would have undermined a key prosecution witness and altered the trial narrative. Strickler does not authorize collapsing Kyles’s contextual materiality test into a sufficiency review; it applies the same reasonable-probability standard while emphasizing case-specific evaluation of how impeachment changes the evidentiary picture. Given the real-world risk of convicting on an unreliably bolstered case—particularly when the State withholds evidence bearing on credibility—AEDPA deference does not excuse a method of analysis this Court has expressly rejected.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Clearly established Brady law requires assessing materiality cumulatively and in the context of the whole case, asking whether there is a “reasonable probability” of a different result—not whether the remaining evidence is legally sufficient. Kyles v. Whitley specifically rejects a sufficiency-of-the-evidence approach and directs courts to consider how suppressed impeachment/exculpatory evidence would alter the overall evidentiary picture and trial narrative. Under AEDPA, § 2254(d)(1) bars relief unless the state court’s application is unreasonable, but if the Maryland appellate court effectively just catalogued inculpatory proof and failed to grapple with the cumulative, case-wide impact of the suppressed evidence on the prosecution’s key witness, that is an unreasonable application of Kyles even under Harrington v. Richter’s “fairminded jurists could disagree” standard. Strickler v. Greene does not permit reducing Brady materiality to sufficiency review; it applies the same reasonable-probability framework on its distinct facts.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Under 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1), a state court unreasonably applies clearly established law when it recites the correct Brady standard but then effectively substitutes a sufficiency-of-the-evidence inquiry for Brady’s “reasonable probability” materiality test. Kyles v. Whitley requires evaluating suppressed evidence cumulatively and in the context of the whole case—including how impeachment can diminish the State’s proof and bolster the defense—not merely tallying remaining inculpatory evidence. If the Maryland appellate court’s analysis turned on whether “substantial” or “strong” evidence still supported guilt even without the suppressed report, that approach conflicts with Kyles’s instruction that materiality is not a sufficiency test and thus is an unreasonable application under AEDPA despite the deference emphasized in Harrington v. Richter. Because the suppressed evidence allegedly undercuts the only testimony linking Martin to the alleged silencer, its cumulative impeachment/exculpatory force plausibly “undermines confidence in the outcome,” satisfying Brady materiality and warranting habeas relief.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under AEDPA, a state court decision is reversible only if it is an “unreasonable application” of clearly established Supreme Court law. 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1); Williams v. Taylor; Harrington v. Richter. Kyles squarely holds that Brady materiality is a cumulative, contextual “reasonable probability” inquiry and “is not a sufficiency of evidence test,” requiring courts to assess the suppressed evidence’s combined effect on the whole case, including how impeachment would weaken the prosecution’s narrative. If the Maryland appellate court effectively upheld nondisclosure by reciting remaining inculpatory evidence without grappling with the cumulative, case-altering force of the suppressed impeachment/exculpatory material, that approach is beyond fairminded disagreement and thus unreasonable under § 2254(d)(1), even accounting for Strickler’s deference to context-specific materiality determinations.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Under AEDPA, a state court unreasonably applies clearly established law when it identifies the correct rule but applies it in a way that no fairminded jurist could defend. 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1); Williams v. Taylor; Harrington v. Richter. Kyles v. Whitley clearly establishes that Brady materiality is not a sufficiency-of-the-evidence test and must be assessed cumulatively, in light of the whole case, including how suppressed impeachment/exculpatory evidence would weaken the prosecution’s narrative and strengthen the defense. If the Maryland appellate court effectively asked only whether there remained “substantial evidence” of guilt rather than performing Kyles’s contextual, cumulative reasonable-probability inquiry, that methodology is contrary to (and an unreasonable application of) Kyles even if the court recited the correct standard, and Strickler does not authorize substituting sufficiency review for Brady materiality.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under Brady v. Maryland and Kyles v. Whitley, materiality turns on whether suppressed evidence creates a “reasonable probability” of a different result when assessed cumulatively and in the context of the whole case—not on whether the remaining evidence is still legally sufficient to convict. If the Maryland appellate court effectively upheld nondisclosure by cataloging inculpatory proof and concluding there was “substantial evidence” anyway, it unreasonably applied clearly established Brady materiality law by failing to account for how the impeachment/exculpatory evidence would have altered the trial narrative and the jury’s assessment of key witnesses. AEDPA, 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1), is highly deferential, but it does not permit a state court to substitute a sufficiency-of-the-evidence inquiry for Kyles’s holistic reasonable-probability analysis; that methodological error can be an “unreasonable application” even if the court recites the correct standard. Strickler v. Greene does not save the state’s approach where the suppressed evidence goes to the credibility of an important witness and the state court does not meaningfully evaluate the cumulative effect on both the prosecution and defense cases.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether, under AEDPA, the Fourth Circuit correctly held that Maryland unreasonably applied clearly established Supreme Court Brady materiality law by treating the suppressed impeachment/exculpatory evidence as immaterial based largely on the strength (sufficiency) of the remaining trial evidence rather than conducting Kyles’s holistic “reasonable probability” analysis.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1) (AEDPA: state decision “contrary to” or “unreasonable application” of clearly established Supreme Court law) as applied to the Due Process Brady doctrine (U.S. Const. amend. XIV) requiring disclosure of material exculpatory/impeachment evidence.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The state officials (petitioners) argue that the Maryland appellate court cited the correct Brady/Kyles materiality standard and reasonably applied it; that any suppressed material was not “material” because the remaining evidence was sufficient to support the verdict; and that the Fourth Circuit improperly reweighed evidence or demanded a more searching analysis than clearly established Supreme Court precedent (including Strickler) requires under AEDPA’s deferential “fairminded jurists could disagree” standard.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Martin (respondent) argues that clearly established Supreme Court law—especially Kyles—requires a cumulative, case-wide materiality assessment that adds the suppressed evidence to the defense side and subtracts the suppressed impeachment force from the prosecution side; that the Maryland appellate court effectively performed an impermissible sufficiency-of-the-evidence analysis by listing remaining inculpatory evidence and declaring the suppression immaterial; that Strickler does not support the State because its facts involved a witness whose impeachment would not have meaningfully undermined the rest of the case; and therefore the state court’s decision was an unreasonable application of Brady/Kyles under § 2254(d)(1).

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson are right that Kyles’s “not a sufficiency test” admonition is substantive and that a court cannot insulate a wrong yardstick by reciting “reasonable probability.” But under Richter and Lockyer, the habeas question is whether the Maryland court’s decision is beyond fairminded disagreement, and I do not read Kyles as clearly establishing that emphasizing the strength of the remaining evidence necessarily converts the inquiry into a forbidden sufficiency test. As Justice Barrett and Justice Alito note, the state court invoked the correct Brady/Kyles standard and can plausibly be read as making an overall confidence-in-the-verdict judgment that considered cumulative impact, even if it articulated that judgment imperfectly. Strickler confirms that suppressed impeachment can be immaterial in a strong case, so absent a clearer indication that Maryland actually applied a different rule, § 2254(d)(1) forecloses the Fourth Circuit’s reweighing.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson press the strongest point: Kyles makes clear Brady materiality is "not a sufficiency of the evidence" test, and AEDPA deference cannot insulate a state court that substantively uses the wrong yardstick. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Alito emphasize, under Harrington v. Richter and Lockyer v. Andrade the question is whether Maryland’s decision was beyond fairminded disagreement, and Kyles does not clearly establish that discussing the strength of the remaining evidence—while expressly invoking the "reasonable probability/undermined confidence" standard—necessarily converts the inquiry into forbidden sufficiency review. Strickler reinforces that considering the whole record, including the case’s overall strength, is part of the materiality judgment; it does not demand any particular "add-to-the-defense-case" narrative format. On an originalist and textualist view of § 2254(d)(1), we cannot treat imperfect reasoning emphasis as equivalent to applying a different rule where the state court can fairly be read as making the verdict-confidence determination Kyles requires.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson make the strongest point that AEDPA deference does not protect a state court that in substance applies the wrong “yardstick,” because Kyles clearly rejects a mere sufficiency-of-the-remaining-evidence approach. But even taking that seriously, I do not think Kyles clearly establishes that a state court’s emphasis on the strength of the unimpeached evidence—while expressly invoking “reasonable probability” and “undermined confidence”—can only be read as a forbidden sufficiency test, rather than a permissible way of explaining why confidence in the verdict remains intact. Under Harrington v. Richter and Lockyer, the question is whether Maryland’s bottom-line application is beyond fairminded disagreement, and as Chief Justice Roberts notes, Strickler confirms that even credibility-related impeachment may be immaterial in a strong case when the verdict-confidence judgment remains reasonable. The Fourth Circuit’s conclusion strikes me as too close to de novo recharacterization of the state court’s analysis, which § 2254(d)(1) does not allow absent a clearer conflict with established Supreme Court law.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s Richter/Lockyer point is the hardest for respondents, and I agree AEDPA does not police a state court’s opinion-writing or forbid mentioning the strength of the remaining evidence. But Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson are right that Kyles clearly establishes a substantive rule: materiality is a cumulative “reasonable probability” inquiry that cannot, in substance, be collapsed into “the rest of the case was strong,” especially when the suppressed evidence bears on credibility and the defense’s ability to test the State’s narrative. Strickler (invoked by Justices Alito and Barrett) permits considering overall case strength, yet it still requires adding the suppressed evidence to the mix and asking whether confidence in the verdict is undermined; a decision that functionally tallies inculpatory proof while discounting the collective impeachment/narrative effect applies the wrong yardstick. On this record, the Fourth Circuit is best understood not as doing de novo reweighing, but as identifying an unreasonable application of Kyles under § 2254(d)(1) even under Richter’s high bar.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s best point—rooted in Richter and Lockyer—is that AEDPA does not require a particular opinion format and permits fairminded disagreement where a state court recites the correct Brady language while discussing the strength of the remaining evidence. But Kyles’s “not a sufficiency test” rule is not about style; it is a substantive yardstick, and Justice Jackson is right that the question is whether the suppressed evidence, taken cumulatively, would have altered the defense’s presentation and the jury’s assessment of credibility, not whether the rest of the case still looks strong in isolation. Strickler does allow case-strength context, yet it still requires integrating the suppressed impeachment into the whole-trial picture; if the state court’s reasoning functionally short-circuits that integration by treating “strong remaining evidence” as dispositive, deference cannot immunize a materially wrong framework. On this record, I continue to think the Fourth Circuit could reasonably conclude the state court unreasonably applied Kyles even under Richter’s demanding standard.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s “wrong yardstick” point is the best rejoinder: AEDPA deference cannot launder a decision that, in substance, replaces Kyles’s cumulative reasonable-probability inquiry with a mere “the rest was strong” sufficiency test. But I remain unpersuaded that the Maryland court’s opinion can only fairly be read that way; as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett stress, it recited the correct “undermines confidence” standard and its emphasis on remaining evidence is plausibly part of that record-wide judgment, not a categorical sufficiency substitute. Kyles clearly forbids treating materiality as equivalent to sufficiency, yet it does not clearly establish a required analytic script (e.g., explicit “add-to-the-defense-case” narration) or a ban on considering the strength of unimpeached evidence when assessing confidence in the verdict. Under Richter and Lockyer, that ambiguity means respondents have not shown the state court’s application was beyond fairminded disagreement, so § 2254(d)(1) bars the Fourth Circuit’s effectively de novo reweighing.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson most forcefully argue that the Maryland court in substance used the forbidden Kyles “sufficiency-of-the-remaining-evidence” yardstick, and I agree AEDPA cannot insulate a decision that truly applies the wrong rule despite reciting the right words. But Chief Justice Roberts’s Richter/Lockyer point remains dispositive for me: unless the state opinion can only fairly be read as a sufficiency test (rather than a verdict-confidence judgment that references remaining-evidence strength), § 2254(d)(1) requires us to deny relief. Kyles clearly rejects sufficiency-as-materiality, yet it does not clearly require a particular “add-to-the-defense-case” analytic format or forbid discussing unimpeached proof as part of the holistic confidence inquiry, and Strickler reinforces that even suppressed impeachment can be immaterial in a case reasonably viewed as still strong. On this record, I cannot say no fairminded jurist could view Maryland as applying the reasonable-probability/undermined-confidence standard, so the Fourth Circuit’s approach risks de novo reweighing.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson make the most serious point: Kyles clearly rejects reducing Brady materiality to a sufficiency-of-the-evidence test, and AEDPA cannot defer to a state court that in substance uses the wrong yardstick. But under Harrington v. Richter and Lockyer v. Andrade (as the Chief Justice emphasizes), § 2254(d)(1) asks whether the Maryland court’s decision is beyond fairminded disagreement, and Kyles does not clearly prescribe any particular “add-to-the-defense-case” analytic form or forbid referencing remaining-evidence strength when the court frames the question as whether confidence in the verdict is undermined. Reading the Maryland opinion charitably, its discussion of the “remaining evidence” can plausibly be part of the verdict-confidence inquiry rather than an impermissible sufficiency substitute, and Strickler supports that even credibility-impeachment may be immaterial in a case a fairminded jurist could still view as strong. Because the Fourth Circuit’s conclusion that Maryland necessarily applied the forbidden sufficiency test is not compelled by clearly established law, I remain with the petitioner.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Alito’s AEDPA point—that Richter/Lockyer bar de novo reweighing and do not demand any particular opinion-writing—does not resolve whether the state court actually applied Kyles’s substantive cumulative materiality framework. I agree with Justice Barrett and Justice Gorsuch that Kyles permits considering the strength of the remaining evidence, but only as part of the counterfactual “confidence in the verdict” inquiry that integrates the suppressed evidence into the defense case; when a court’s analysis functionally becomes “the rest was strong,” it collapses materiality into sufficiency in the way Kyles forbids. Strickler’s recognition that strong cases can render impeachment immaterial does not authorize skipping the credibility-centered, adversarial-testing question that suppressed impeachment uniquely affects. On this record, I continue to think the Fourth Circuit could reasonably view Maryland’s decision as an unreasonable application of Kyles’s yardstick, not mere disagreement with outcome under § 2254(d)(1).

John Roberts.reasoning: Under AEDPA, 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1), the question is not whether the Fourth Circuit (or this Court) would conduct the Brady/Kyles materiality inquiry differently, but whether the state court’s adjudication was an objectively unreasonable application of clearly established Supreme Court law such that no fairminded jurist could agree. Although Kyles v. Whitley emphasizes that materiality “is not a sufficiency of evidence test” and requires a cumulative assessment, a state court does not act unreasonably merely by discussing the strength of the remaining evidence so long as it invokes and applies the “reasonable probability” standard in substance. Given Harrington v. Richter and Lockyer v. Andrade’s insistence on broad leeway to state courts and on not converting § 2254(d)(1) into de novo review, I would not hold that Maryland’s analysis crossed the high threshold from arguable error into unreasonableness.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Under AEDPA, federal habeas relief is barred unless the state court’s decision was an objectively unreasonable application of clearly established Supreme Court law, not merely incorrect. 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1); Harrington v. Richter, 562 U.S. 86, 102 (2011). If the Maryland court identified Brady/Kyles’s “reasonable probability” materiality standard and then concluded the suppressed impeachment/exculpatory evidence did not undermine confidence in the verdict, Richter and Lockyer v. Andrade require deference so long as fairminded jurists could agree with that application—even if the state court’s analysis emphasized the strength of the remaining evidence. Because Kyles v. Whitley does not clearly establish a required level of analytical detail or forbid a state court from relying heavily on remaining-evidence strength as part of its materiality judgment, the Fourth Circuit exceeded § 2254(d)(1) by substituting its own reweighing for the state court’s permissible assessment.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Under AEDPA, federal habeas relief is barred unless the state court’s decision was an “unreasonable application” of clearly established Supreme Court law, meaning it was so lacking in justification that no fairminded jurist could agree. 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1); Harrington v. Richter, 562 U.S. 86, 102-03 (2011). Although Kyles requires a cumulative “reasonable probability” materiality assessment, a state court does not act unreasonably merely by emphasizing the strength of the remaining evidence so long as it articulates and applies the Brady materiality standard in substance, and Strickler confirms that not every suppressed impeachment item is material where the overall case remains strong. Given Richter’s demanding deference and the risk of turning Brady into a de novo reweighing exercise in federal court, the Fourth Circuit should not have displaced Maryland’s judgment absent a clear, outcome-determinative misapplication of Kyles beyond fairminded disagreement.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Under AEDPA, 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1) still requires deference only to state-court decisions that reasonably apply clearly established Supreme Court law, and Kyles v. Whitley clearly establishes that Brady materiality is a cumulative, holistic “reasonable probability” inquiry—not a sufficiency-of-the-evidence test that simply inventories remaining inculpatory proof. If the Maryland appellate court treated the suppressed impeachment/exculpatory evidence as immaterial largely because other evidence was “substantial,” it repeated the very error Kyles rejected by failing to add the suppressed evidence to the defense case and account for how it would have undermined the prosecution’s presentation. While Harrington v. Richter cautions that relief is limited to errors beyond fairminded disagreement, a state court’s effective substitution of sufficiency analysis for Kyles’s materiality framework can be an “unreasonable application” of clearly established law, particularly where the suppressed evidence could have altered how a jury assessed credibility and reasonable doubt. Given Brady’s due process focus on fairness and the integrity of verdicts, the Fourth Circuit correctly found the state court’s approach unreasonable under § 2254(d)(1).

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Under 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1), AEDPA deference is substantial, but it does not permit a state court to substitute a sufficiency-of-the-evidence inquiry for Brady materiality. Kyles v. Whitley clearly establishes that materiality requires a cumulative, case-wide “reasonable probability” assessment of how the suppressed evidence would have aided the defense and undermined the prosecution, not whether the remaining evidence could still support the verdict. Where the state appellate court’s analysis largely tallies up inculpatory evidence and declares the suppression immaterial, it unreasonably applies that clearly established rule, even under Harrington v. Richter’s “fairminded jurists could disagree” standard. The Fourth Circuit therefore correctly held that Maryland’s approach was an unreasonable application of clearly established Brady/Kyles law.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Under AEDPA, a federal court may grant relief only if the state court’s decision was not just wrong but an “unreasonable application” of clearly established Supreme Court law, beyond fairminded disagreement. 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1); Harrington v. Richter. Kyles requires a cumulative “reasonable probability” materiality inquiry, but it does not demand any particular style of opinion-writing, and a state court does not act unreasonably merely by emphasizing the strength of the remaining evidence while citing the correct Brady/Kyles standard. Given Richter’s deference and the leeway recognized in Strickler’s application of Brady materiality to the record as a whole, the Fourth Circuit went too far by effectively insisting on a more “nuanced” or “exhaustive” analysis than clearly established precedent requires.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under AEDPA, federal habeas relief is available only if the state court’s decision was an “unreasonable application” of clearly established Supreme Court law, not merely incorrect, and relief must be denied if fairminded jurists could disagree. 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1); Harrington v. Richter. Although Kyles v. Whitley makes clear that Brady materiality is not a bare sufficiency-of-the-evidence inquiry and requires a cumulative “reasonable probability” assessment, the Maryland appellate court cited the correct Brady/Kyles standard and its discussion of the remaining evidence can reasonably be understood as part of assessing whether nondisclosure undermined confidence in the verdict. Given the deference demanded by Richter and the Court’s recognition in Strickler v. Greene that not every undisclosed impeachment item is material when the overall case remains strong, the Fourth Circuit went too far in treating the state court’s analysis as beyond the bounds of reasonable application rather than within the range of permissible disagreement.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Under 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1), the question is not whether the federal court would find Brady materiality de novo, but whether the state court’s adjudication was an objectively unreasonable application of clearly established law such that no fairminded jurist could agree. Although Kyles v. Whitley makes clear that materiality “is not a sufficiency of evidence test,” it also requires a contextual judgment about whether the suppressed evidence creates a “reasonable probability” of a different result, and AEDPA permits state courts to apply that standard without any particular analytic form so long as the correct rule is identified and reasonably applied. Given the state court’s citation to the Brady/Kyles standard and the deference mandated by Harrington v. Richter and Lockyer v. Andrade, I would hold the Fourth Circuit too readily treated the state court’s discussion of remaining evidence as a forbidden sufficiency test rather than a permissible way to explain why there was no reasonable probability of a different verdict.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under AEDPA, a state court unreasonably applies clearly established law when it invokes the correct Brady/Bagley words but effectively substitutes a sufficiency-of-the-remaining-evidence rationale for Kyles’s required cumulative “reasonable probability” assessment. Kyles v. Whitley makes clear that materiality “is not a sufficiency of evidence test” and requires evaluating suppressed impeachment/exculpatory evidence collectively, adding it to the defense case and accounting for its effect on the prosecution’s proof; a decision that largely lists remaining inculpatory evidence and declares the suppression immaterial can therefore be an unreasonable application under 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1). While Harrington v. Richter and Lockyer v. Andrade demand deference and allow room for fairminded disagreement, deference does not permit a state court to apply the wrong analytic framework to the Brady materiality inquiry. Given the due process and procedural-fairness stakes in a criminal prosecution—especially where suppressed evidence bears on the credibility of key witnesses—the Fourth Circuit’s conclusion that Maryland unreasonably applied Kyles is consistent with clearly established Supreme Court law.
